name: Talavera
basis: why: hand-painted tin-glazed tiles, palette limited by the kiln; how: ground colour by brightness, four-way flower with hand wobble, glaze shine

lumenary.blurb: Hand-painted tin-glazed tiles from Puebla, Mexico. Each tile takes its ground from the light in your picture, from cobalt through green and orange to white, and carries a four-way flower in contrasting colours.

facts.from: Puebla, Mexico, descended from Spanish majolica
facts.bestOn: Colourful pictures with warm and cool areas

why: Talavera is painted by hand, so no two tiles are quite alike: the motif sits a little off-centre, a little tilted, and the line wavers. Its palette of cobalt, yellow, green and orange is limited by what survives the kiln. Each tile here takes its ground from the light in the picture, from cobalt in the shadows to white glaze in the lights.
how: Make a tile for every cell of a grid and choose its ground by brightness, from cobalt in the shadows through green, orange and yellow to white glaze.
Paint two accent colours on each ground, chosen to contrast: yellow and white on cobalt, for example, and cobalt with orange on white.
Let the warmth of the picture at that tile (red above blue) decide which of the two accents leads.
Paint a four-way flower or star, offset and tilted slightly by a hand wobble.
Add grout lines and glaze shine.
history: Talavera de Puebla descends from Spanish majolica, brought to New Spain in the sixteenth century, and it also took on Indigenous and Asian influences. It has a protected designation of origin. In 2019 UNESCO added the artisanal Talavera of Puebla and Tlaxcala, together with the ceramics of Talavera de la Reina and El Puente del Arzobispo in Spain, to its list of intangible heritage.
uses: Wall tiles, sinks and kitchen ware
terms: Tin-glazed pottery painted with bright colours.
A legal protection for products made in a particular place by tradition.
An oven used to fire pottery.
paragraphs: Talavera de Puebla is tin-glazed earthenware with a protected name. It descends from Spanish majolica, and its palette of cobalt, yellow, green and orange is limited by what survives the kiln. The tiles are painted by hand, so no two are quite alike: the motif is a little off-centre, a little tilted, and the line wavers. The program makes a tile for every cell of a grid and chooses the ground by brightness, from cobalt in the shadows through green, orange and yellow to white glaze in the lights.

Two accent colours are painted on each ground, chosen to contrast: yellow and white on cobalt, for example, and cobalt with orange on white. Which of the two leads is decided by the warmth of the picture at that tile (red above blue means warm), so the hues of your picture reach the tile in a small way. A tile carries either an eight-petal flower with four leaves in its corners, or two eight-pointed stars with four round bosses. A thin painted border runs inside the edge, and a glaze shine covers the lot.

equations.note: The ground of a tile from its blurred brightness t.
The vertices of an eight-pointed star: tips at R₁ and notches at R₂ (0.85 u and 0.42 u for the large star, 0.5 u and 0.26 u for the small one).
The warm-or-cool rule: R and B are the red and blue values of the picture’s boosted colour at the tile.

presets.text: Star motifs give a more geometric, Moorish look.
A little hand wobble keeps tiles alive; a lot makes them playful.
Wide grout makes each tile stand alone.
